History:
• 27-year-old male (Dan Choudhry) presents with 3-day history of profuse watery diarrhoea, occurring “almost every hour” while awake.  
• Onset: Mon/Tue this week; not improving.  
• Stool: Watery, no blood or mucus reported.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Crampy mid-lower abdominal pain, colicky, 6/10, precedes bowel actions and then eases.  
  – Nausea; occasional vomiting, especially after milk ingestion.  
  – Subjective fever/feeling “hot.”  
  – Slightly reduced urine frequency.  
• Brother has had similar illness for 5 days → possible infectious exposure.  
• Triggers/aggravators: Milk worsens nausea/vomiting; fluids feel as if they “go straight through.”  
• Relievers: None noted; using paracetamol for pain/fever.  
• Last solid food: Lunch today—resulted in loose stool soon after.  
• No recent travel; often eats takeaway food.  

Past Medical History:
• No chronic illnesses reported.  
• Medications: Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented); no other regular medications.  
• Allergies: No known drug allergies.  
• Family history: Father with stage III colon cancer; brother currently ill with similar diarrhoeal illness.  
• Social: Lives with mother and sister; office worker (government). Social smoker (occasional, mainly weekends); alcohol socially, binge episodes 1–2×/month.  

Physical Examination:
(NOTE: Video consultation—no objective exam performed)  
• General: Appears unwell via video; alert and oriented.  
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• Abdominal exam: Not performed.  
• No other systems examined.  

Impression:
Acute infectious gastroenteritis (likely viral) with risk of dehydration.  
Supporting DDx consistent with transcript:  
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis (high likelihood—abrupt onset, similar household case, watery stool).  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis (medium likelihood—takeaway food, feverish).  
3. Transient post-infectious lactose intolerance (milk triggers vomiting).  

Management Plan:
• Oral rehydration: Advise OTC Dioralyte/other oral rehydration solution; encourage frequent small sips of clear fluids.  
• Diet: Start with clear liquids, progress to soft foods (soups, mashed foods) as tolerated; avoid dairy initially.  
• Medications: Continue paracetamol as needed for pain/fever (dose not documented); avoid alcohol until recovery.  
• Monitoring: Watch for signs of dehydration (reduced urine, dizziness, persistent vomiting, inability to keep fluids).  
• Safety-net: If symptoms do not improve within 48 hours, worsen, or dehydration develops, patient to call back for further assessment (possible labs, stool culture, IV fluids).  
• No prescription issued today.  

Patient Summary:
27-year-old otherwise healthy man with 3-day profuse watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, nausea, and subjective fever—likely acute viral gastroenteritis acquired at home. Advised on oral rehydration, soft diet, symptomatic relief, and to re-contact if no improvement within 48 hours.  

Key Takeaways:
• Use Dioralyte or similar oral rehydration salts regularly; keep urine pale-yellow.  
• Clear fluids and soft foods only; avoid dairy, alcohol, and heavy meals until settled.  
• Seek medical help if symptoms persist >48 hrs or any dehydration signs appear.  

Next Steps:
• Patient to obtain oral rehydration solution today.  
• Re-assessment (telephone or in-person) in 48 hrs if no improvement.  
• Consider stool testing, blood work, and IV fluids if deteriorates or fails to improve.
